title: Paramitas – #4 Effort
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: The main teaching of this Soto Zen dharma talk emphasizes the importance of effort or zeal in Zen practice, which involves developing spiritual strength and stamina to persist in one's practice despite challenges and discomforts. This requires discipline, self-awareness, and adaptability, particularly as we age or face physical limitations. By cultivating mindfulness and compassion, we can find a balance between our body's needs and our spiritual aspirations, leading to greater clarity and focus in all aspects of life.

sentences.text: **Shuko Edie Norton:** *[unclear: "Enhancement house"], penetrating and perfect dharma, to taste the truth of the dharma.*
Paramitas again tonight. [unclear: "Visual A"] for those of us who learn by reading or seeing.
I'm going to talk especially about effort, the fourth one.
The paramitas, or perfections, were derived from the classical Buddhist three-part teaching of sila, which means morality; samadhi, which means absorption or meditation; and prajna, wisdom.
A few centuries later, Mahayana Buddhism developed the teachings and expanded the paramitas to six, which is up here.
Generosity, or giving, which is perfected when there is no difference in status between the giver and the receiver.
The giver has to have a receiver in order to give, and the receiver has to have a giver in order to receive.
They're reciprocal, they're not one on top of the other, which we as human beings tend to forget.
Morality, or ethical conduct, ethics: the natural expression, actually, of an awakening mind.
Morality happens as we awaken.
Patience, or forbearance, that is tolerance toward working with difficulties.
Forbearance, I think, is a really good way to think about patience, because forbearance means you don't immediately react to something that you dislike.
You're forbearing, you wait, you re-observe, you reflect before you act, so I think that's a really good word for it.
Effort, or zeal, the spiritual strength and stamina to persist in the practice.
Meditation, the settled, focused state of samadhi, and wisdom, the experiential insight into the empty nature of all phenomena.
That is, everything is always changing, so nothing has a permanent condition or nature.
Four more paramitas were added later, and those were skillful means, vow or commitment, powers or psychic abilities, and knowledge.
These are the additional ones that we're not studying at this point.
The paramitas, or perfections, are not fixed rules for conduct.
They are inspirations, practices, or ways to live and perfect our lives.
And by practicing the perfections, we also help others to practice them too and perfect their lives, so everyone is together on this.
Tonight I want to talk about the fourth paramita, probably the dullest one here, the least inspiring: effort, or zeal, or even enthusiasm.
What is meant by this paramita?

At the Rinzai temple in Japan, Sogenji, where I practiced 23 years ago for a year, we had a [unclear: "ma'a"] sesshin every month, a seven-day sesshin every month, and always in the [unclear: "dharmata"] and in the doksans, the roshi would repeatedly admonish us to put all our effort into zazen, to try our hardest, to focus on our breath or on our koan.
Effort, effort, effort was the watchword at Sogenji.
Living in Japan, where I was teaching English at a small university, I came to realize that effort was a central value in Japanese culture.
Time and time again, I would see on television a new government official or a new head of an organization promising to do his best or her best at their new job.
They would work hard to live up to their responsibilities.
Living there, in this very earnest culture, I discovered that I was working really, really hard, trying very, very hard at everything I was doing.
The Japanese see their individual effort as contributing necessarily to the whole group's benefit.
For a Westerner like myself, it was a strain always to be trying so hard when I really didn't have a particular reason to do it, a particular group reason or expectation.
Soto Zen teachers don't emphasize effort as much as the Japanese Rinzai roshi did, but at our sesshins, students are definitely urged to follow the full schedule fully.
Not to miss any periods of zazen, not to pick and choose.
Completely following the schedule was urged repeatedly at Tassajara Zen Monastery, where Chris and I spent three months, a couple of years ago, in the practice period there.
Repeatedly, the abbess admonished us to come in the morning first thing and always come in the evening last thing.
And I began to wonder if people were skipping out on these things because she said it so often.
But this admonition was for a good reason.
Following the schedule fully at a sesshin or practice period removes individual choice.
It thus removes from us our habit of having preferences.
No choices, no preferences.
Kind of works in that direction anyway.
Following the schedule also gives us the opportunity to experience what making a big effort is like, especially when you're growing more and more tired during sesshin as the days go on.
So what does this paramita of effort mean in our American Zen practice?
I don't have any official or inside information on this, but I do have some experience and observations on the subject.
First, Zen practice takes effort because for the most part, people, Americans, don't come to Zen practice because they think it might be fun or give us some time off.
In my experience anyway, most people come to Zen out of a need to calm down, to find some purpose or some way of putting their life together better, stabilizing, balancing, living more contentedly.
This search may not be conscious, but it usually underlies why people do come here.

Forty and fifty years ago, when Zen Buddhism was still new in America and therefore considered quite weird, a person coming to Zen needed a pretty strong motivation to try something as strange as that.

It isn't the case that way so much anymore, but because the concepts and premises of Buddhism are so different from Western concepts about reality, it still takes some determination and independence of mind to step into a Zendo and to come back to it.

A second observation about effort is that Zen practice takes effort because for Americans and Westerners in general, the traditional seated positions in zazen are physically challenging to many of us.
Our knees and hips and backs have not been shaped by sitting on the floor since we were infants, as is the case in Asian countries.
We have grown up sitting in chairs and sleeping in beds that are raised off the floor.

The physical practice of zazen requires effort, determination, and patience as we suffer through whatever pain and time it takes for our bodies to adjust, for our joints and tendons to release so we can sit more comfortably.
Sometimes this takes years to accomplish.
A third observation is the concept of meditation, especially the Soto Zen concept of Shikantaza, which means just sitting.
It's a Japanese word that means like only sitting or maybe pure sitting, something like that.
We usually call it just sitting.
Just sitting and not thinking about something.
What does it mean to just sit and not think?
What are we supposed to do with our mental activity?
Well, this is what takes a lot of energy and a lot of enthusiasm: to learn this practice and continue doing it.
Let's talk a little bit about enthusiasm.

In order to be willing to do the hard work of becoming aware of our mind's activity and to return our attention again and again, endless times, to our breath or our body, we have to be enthusiastic about this practice we have taken up.
We have to believe in its worth.
We have to have good reason to stick with this challenging practice.
We have to be convinced that it is beneficial.
Thus, energy and enthusiasm are necessary elements of practice.
And the interesting thing about energy is that zazen collects and concentrates it.

Do you notice, after we've sat together for two or three periods on Wednesday evenings, that when we go out in the lobby, there's a lot of energy there, a lot of happiness that we can't seem to contain?
This is what happens for most people at the end of a sesshin.
Even though the sesshin might have been tiring, often people are very energized and joyful at its end, not just because it's over.

When I was first sitting at a sesshin, I learned that I had to be careful who I talked to fairly soon after, because my energy was so high I didn't know what was going to come out of my mouth, and often embarrassing things came out.
So I learned to just hold back a little bit before I talked to people, regular friends and so forth.
This was the energy I had collected through zazen.

Of course, sometimes long sitting can be very tiring as well, and each of us needs to take good care of our own bodies and ourselves when this happens, so as not to overdo it and thereby lose the many benefits of zazen, such as insight and peace and joy.
I had another example years ago of how much energy can get collected in zazen.

I was taking a couple of years of training in tea ceremony, and one day I was going to have my class that evening, and so before I went to work I practiced going through all the moves that the tea server does.
I was supposed to perform that in the evening at the class, and I got into the car, and this was during the fall or winter in California, so it was not real cold but cool and so forth.
So I was driving to work on the freeway and my window kept steaming up and I couldn't figure out what that was for.
I realized it was because I had been so intense in going and rehearsing this ceremony.
Well, that's what happens in zazen too.
We get really hot.
So if we jumped in our car right away we might all be steaming up our windows, I don't know.
The fourth observation I have about effort is that perhaps it is most obviously expressed in a discipline that we must develop in order to maintain our zazen practice once we have begun it.
It takes discipline to start and maintain zazen practice at home and to come regularly to the Zendo to practice with the Sangha.
It also takes discipline to study Buddhism, Buddhist teachings, through reading, classes, attending Dharma talks.
Studying Buddhism takes self-discipline because many of its concepts are arcane and subtle and difficult to understand.
Some are even impossible to understand cognitively, which is the way we mostly access information.
So we have to cultivate the discipline of patience with ourselves as well as the ability to tolerate ambiguity and our confusion when studying or listening to the teachings.
This self-discipline is big and essential for [unclear: "its end students"].
Effort is also required to learn the forms and continuously practice and refine them.
Gassho when entering the Zendo, gassho before and after changing positions, bowing full bows to the floor, when to face inward, when to face toward the altar.
All these different forms that we learn and follow take attention and energy to do.
They all teach us, though, to pay attention to the present moment.
That's the purpose of them: to pay attention to what is now.
When we're paying attention to what's going on now, we're not suffering about what might happen or what did happen.
We're just dealing with what is here.
So these forms have a definite practical purpose and result.
Then there is our bodhisattva practice.
One of Soto Zen's most important concepts and practices, the archetype and vow or commitment to give up one's own enlightenment for the sake of other people, to help them become enlightened.
The bodhisattva vow is the essence of the paramita of effort.
Saving all sentient beings, an impossible thing to do.
Therefore, you need great energy and zeal and effort to do so.
Complete commitment to practice, no half-heartedness, living wholeheartedly for and with others in any and all ways that we can.
That's what the bodhisattva vow means.
Shantideva, in *The Way of the Bodhisattva*, you remember when we were studying that, sometimes spoke of the bodhisattva as a warrior going into battle.
This felt uncomfortable to some of our people who would like to think of the bodhisattva mostly in terms of compassion and generosity and kindness.
But Shantideva was referring to the great zeal and wholehearted commitment that a bodhisattva must have in order to make and sustain selfless effort for the benefit of all.
So the paramita of effort is available to us all in Zen practice and necessary to sustaining our individual practice as well as our sangha life.
Many of you volunteer to do different jobs, different roles for our sangha, and this is bodhisattva practice.
This takes effort and dedication and self-discipline, and we deeply appreciate everyone's contribution in this way.
A final note about effort.
There can come a time or times when the strong effort of traditional Zen practice can be deleterious to the individual.
Times when sitting long sesshin days or getting little sleep is harmful to the individual student because of a physical condition or injury or illness or, in my case, old age.
The Buddhist admonition that old age, sickness, and death are in the cards for all of us eventually is not just a saying.

I have discovered in the past couple of years that as I've definitely moved into old age, though not actually sick, I do have limitations physically, new ones, so that now it is unhealthy for me to sit for long periods or not get enough sleep.

So my new discipline and effort have become learning to be very mindful of my body and its needs at any given time and to work with those needs when it means I cannot sit as I used to on this zafu or cannot sit for long hours.
No longer being able to participate as I had for 40 years of my Zen practice is a real loss for me, but I must accept the new reality of my aging body.
And I'm learning to use my effort or zeal for practice to develop new ways to participate.
I'm using effort now to discipline myself, not to throw myself into following the schedule fully, completely, but to consider my body's needs and weave them as priorities into my practice.
There is always more to learn and do.
And I have to say, after throwing the body and mind fully into the schedule for many, many years, it's the kind of hard habit to break.
I feel guilty.
I feel ashamed.
I feel that people will think I'm a bad Buddhist student and that kind of thing.
All those things run through, but I have to do it, and I'm trying to do it, and I'm making something of the way.

I hope you will reflect on effort as a paramita that you have and express in your own Zen practice, and appreciate the beautiful opportunity Zen gives us to perfect ourselves and in doing so to help others toward their own perfection.
If there are questions or comments, we have a little bit of time for that.
A couple minutes.
**Participant:** You spoke about effort mostly in the framework of Zen practice, but since we practice everyday Zen, how do you move that into the everyday world?
How to deal with effort in the everyday world.

**Shuko Edie Norton:** I think it's very much like Zen practice, in that you figure out what it is that you really want to spend your effort and energy on, and how much you can do and how much you can expend and what's too much.
You find your way, your parameters in that.
One of the things I think that's really wonderful about Zen is it does help us to figure out what it is we really want to do and focus on and practice our life.
It really kind of clears the clutter.
Not just the zazen period itself, but just the way that we learn to think about things.
It gets easier and easier to do that.
It's also true that we change over time and get new conditions and new limitations sometimes.
I'm certainly feeling that.
But we can figure it out because we know how to focus and find our heart in our life, I think.
*With the true merit of Buddha's way*
*Beings are numberless* *To save them* *Delusions are inexhaustible* *I vow to end them* *Our gates are boundless* *I vow to end them*
